content: This is the third updated version of a Cochrane review originally published in 2003 and updated in 2007. Morphine has been widely used for many years as a primary treatment for cancer-related pain. Oral morphine, available in both immediate-release (MIR) and modified-release (Mm/r) formulations, remains the preferred analgesic for managing moderate to severe cancer pain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of oral morphine in alleviating cancer pain and to assess the frequency and severity of associated adverse events. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared oral morphine with either placebo or other active treatments in adults and children with cancer pain. Trials with fewer than 10 participants were excluded. The search strategy involved multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to October 2015, as well as ClinicalTrials.gov. Data extraction was performed by one reviewer and verified by another. Due to insufficient comparable data, meta-analysis could not be conducted, and numbers needed to treat (NNTs) for analgesic effects were not calculated. However, data on the proportion of participants achieving no worse than mild pain or treatment success were extracted when available. This update identified seven new studies, of which six were excluded, and one is ongoing. In total, the review includes 62 studies with 4241 participants. Thirty-six of these studies employed a cross-over design, with trial durations ranging from one to 15 days, most commonly seven days per treatment arm. The included studies were judged to have a high risk of bias due to poor reporting of randomization and allocation concealment methods. The primary outcomes assessed were participant-reported pain intensity and pain relief. Fifteen studies compared Mm/r with MIR formulations, while 14 studies compared different strengths of Mm/r, including six that evaluated 24-hour modified-release products. Fifteen studies compared Mm/r with other opioids, and six compared MIR with other opioids. Additional comparisons included oral Mm/r versus rectal Mm/r, MIR versus MIR via different routes, and morphine versus non-opioid analgesics. One study compared oral morphine with epidural morphine. In the previous update, a standard of no worse than mild pain was defined as a score of 30/100 mm or less on a visual analogue scale (VAS) or equivalent measures. Eighteen studies achieved this level of pain relief on average, and no study reported a failure to achieve good pain relief. Among 17 studies reporting individual participant outcomes, 96% of participants (362/377) achieved no worse than mild pain, and 63% (400/638) achieved treatment success. Morphine was found to be an effective analgesic for cancer pain, with no significant differences in pain relief between Mm/r and MIR formulations. Modified-release morphine was effective for 12or 24-hour dosing, depending on the formulation. Daily doses ranged from 25 mg to 2000 mg, with an average dose between 100 mg and 250 mg. Dose titration was performed with both MIR and Mm/r products. However, a small proportion of participants did not achieve adequate pain relief with morphine. Adverse events were common and predictable, leading approximately 6% of participants to discontinue treatment due to intolerable side effects. The quality of evidence was generally poor, as many studies were old, small, and primarily conducted for regulatory purposes to demonstrate equivalence between formulations. Most trials included fewer than 100 participants and lacked sufficient data for meta-analysis. Only a few studies reported the proportion of participants achieving good pain relief, but where reported, over 90% experienced no worse than mild pain within a short time frame. The review highlights the wide dose range of morphine used in studies and the small percentage of participants unable to tolerate oral morphine. It also underscores the variability in study designs and the inconsistency of cross-over trials. Many trials used titration to achieve adequate analgesia before crossing participants over, but it was unclear whether these studies were adequately powered to detect clinical differences between formulations or comparator drugs. The conclusions of this review remain unchanged. Oral morphine continues to be an effective and reliable treatment for cancer pain. New studies included in the previous update confirmed that modified-release morphine can be titrated to achieve effective pain relief. Qualitative evidence suggests that oral morphine has comparable efficacy to other available opioids.
